config.title: Build a debounced search input

intro.title: Build a debounced search input
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a search input field that delays sending requests until the user stops typing, preventing excessive API calls. You'll learn about the core programming concept of debouncing, which helps optimize performance by grouping rapid events into a single action. The main technologies involved are JavaScript functions, event listeners, and the setTimeout and clearTimeout methods. By the end, you'll have a functional, efficient search component that improves user experience in real-time applications.
intro.usecase: Debounced search inputs are essential in modern web applications where real-time filtering is required without overwhelming servers or degrading user experience. You'll see this pattern in e-commerce sites like Amazon or eBay, where search suggestions appear as you type without sending excessive API requests. Dashboard interfaces with live data filtering, such as analytics tools or admin panels, use debouncing to smoothly update charts and tables. Even social media platforms implement debounced search when filtering friends lists or searching through posts, ensuring responsive UI while managing network efficiency.

objectives: Construct a controlled input component to capture user search queries.
Initialize and manage state for the search input value and debounced results.
Implement a debounce function to delay the execution of search logic.
Integrate the debounce function with an event handler to control API call frequency.
Render search results dynamically based on the debounced query.
Configure a cleanup mechanism to cancel pending debounced calls on component unmount.
Apply the debounced search pattern to optimize performance in a real-time filtering scenario.

steps.title: Import React and useState
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from the 'react' library.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in both React and useState from 'react'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: importing React and a hook
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have React and useState available to use in your component.
successCriteria: React and useState are imported from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and useState.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're importing both React and useState from 'react'.
steps.feedbackWrong: That's not quite right. You need to import React and useState from 'react'.

steps.title: Create the SearchInput component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named SearchInput that returns null for now.
steps.hint: Define a function called SearchInput that returns null.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create the SearchInput component here
steps.expectedOutcome: A SearchInput component function is defined and returns null.
successCriteria: The SearchInput component is created and returns null.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure the component is named exactly 'SearchInput' and returns null.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you've defined a function named SearchInput and it returns null.

steps.title: Initialize search query state
steps.instruction: Inside your SearchInput component, use useState to create a state variable called 'query' initialized to an empty string.
steps.hint: Call useState with an empty string as the initial value, and destructure the returned array into 'query' and 'setQuery'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: initializing a state variable
const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a state variable 'query' that can hold the current search input value.
successCriteria: The component uses useState to declare a 'query' state variable initialized to an empty string.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using useState to create a 'query' variable initialized to an empty string inside the component.
steps.feedbackWrong: Inside the SearchInput component, use useState to create a state variable called 'query' with an initial value of an empty string.

steps.title: Initialize search results state
steps.instruction: Inside the SearchInput component, use useState to create a state variable named 'results' with an initial value of an empty array.
steps.hint: Add a second useState call after your existing query state. The state variable should be named 'results' and initialized as [].
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: initializing a state variable for an array
const [items, setItems] = useState([]);
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have two state variables: 'query' for the search input and 'results' to store search results.
successCriteria: A state variable named 'results' is declared using useState with an initial value of an empty array.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you're using useState to declare a state variable named 'results' with an initial value of [].
steps.feedbackWrong: add a second useState call to create a state variable named 'results' initialized as an empty array.

steps.title: Create handleInputChange handler
steps.instruction: Inside your SearchInput component, define a function named handleInputChange that takes an event parameter and updates the query state with the event's target value.
steps.hint: The function should call setQuery with event.target.value. You can define it as a regular function or arrow function.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a handleInputChange function that updates the query state when called with an input event.
successCriteria: A function named handleInputChange is defined, takes an event parameter, and calls setQuery with event.target.value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your function is named handleInputChange, takes an event parameter, and calls setQuery with event.target.value.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try again. You need to define a function named handleInputChange that updates the query state with the input value.

steps.title: Create performSearch helper function
steps.instruction: Inside your SearchInput component, create a helper function named performSearch that takes a query parameter and updates the search results state with mock data based on that query.
steps.hint: Define a function that uses the setResults state setter to update results with an array of mock search items. You can simulate API results by returning hardcoded data.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now has a performSearch function that will later be used to simulate searching with the current query.
successCriteria: A function named performSearch is defined inside the component, takes a query parameter, and calls setResults with mock data.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you define a function named performSearch that takes a query parameter and updates the results state.
steps.feedbackWrong: The performSearch function is missing or doesn't match the requirements. Check that it's defined inside the component and updates the results state.

steps.title: Create debounce function
steps.instruction: Create a function named debounce that takes a callback function and a delay in milliseconds as parameters, and returns a debounced version of the callback.
steps.hint: The debounce function should return a new function that will execute the callback only after the specified delay has passed without being called again.
steps.expectedOutcome: A debounce function is defined inside the component, ready to be used to delay the search execution.
successCriteria: The debounce function is created with parameters for callback and delay, and returns a debounced function.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your debounce function takes both callback and delay parameters and returns a new function.
steps.feedbackWrong: The debounce function isn't quite right. It should accept a callback and delay, then return a function that delays execution.

steps.title: Create debouncedSearch handler
steps.instruction: Create a handler function called debouncedSearch that uses your debounce function to wrap the performSearch function.
steps.hint: Define a new function that calls debounce with performSearch and a delay (e.g., 500ms).
steps.expectedOutcome: A debouncedSearch function is defined inside the component, ready to be used with the input.
successCriteria: The debouncedSearch function is created and uses the debounce function to wrap performSearch.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure debouncedSearch uses the debounce function and wraps performSearch.
steps.feedbackWrong: The debouncedSearch handler is missing or not correctly implemented. It should use the debounce function to wrap performSearch.

steps.title: Add input element and wire onChange
steps.instruction: Inside the component's return statement, add an input element with value={query} and onChange={handleInputChange}.
steps.hint: The input element should be a self-closing JSX tag with the value and onChange attributes set to the state and handler you created earlier.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will render a text input field that displays the current query value and updates it when the user types.
successCriteria: An input element is added inside the div
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added an input element, but check that it has both value={query} and onChange={handleInputChange} attributes.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try adding an input element with value={query} and onChange={handleInputChange} inside the div.

steps.title: Display search results
steps.instruction: Add a div element below the input to display the search results array.
steps.hint: Use the results state variable to render the results. You can map through the results array to display each item.
steps.expectedOutcome: The search results will be displayed as a list below the input field when results are available.
successCriteria: A div element is added that maps through the results array and displays each item.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some code to display results, but it might not be complete. Make sure you're mapping through the results array and returning a div for each item.
